{{Short description|Memoryless property of a stochastic process}}
{{about|the property of a stochastic process|the class of properties of a finitely presented group|Adian–Rabin theorem}}
[[File:Wiener process 3d.png|thumb|A single realisation of three-dimensional [[Brownian motion]] for times 0 ≤ t ≤ 2. Brownian motion has the Markov property, as the displacement of the particle does not depend on its past displacements.]]

In [[probability theory]] and [[statistics]], the '''Markov property''' is the [[memoryless]] property of a [[stochastic process]], which means that its future evolution is independent of its history. It is named after the [[Russia]]n [[mathematician]] [[Andrey Markov]]. The term '''strong Markov property''' is similar to the Markov property, except that the meaning of "present" is defined in terms of a [[random variable]] known as a [[stopping time]].

The term '''Markov assumption''' is used to describe a model where the Markov property is assumed to hold, such as a [[hidden Markov model]].

A [[Markov random field]] extends this property to two or more dimensions or to random variables defined for an interconnected network of items.<ref>[[Yadolah Dodge|Dodge, Yadolah]]. (2006) ''The Oxford Dictionary of Statistical Terms'', [[Oxford University Press]]. {{isbn|0-19-850994-4}}</ref> An example of a model for such a field is the [[Ising model]].

A discrete-time stochastic process satisfying the Markov property is known as a [[Markov chain]].

==Introduction==

A stochastic process has the Markov property if the [[conditional probability distribution]] of future states of the process (conditional on both past and present values) depends only upon the present state; that is, given the present, the future does not depend on the past. A process with this property is said to be '''Markov''' or '''Markovian''' and known as a '''[[Markov process]]'''. Two famous classes of Markov process are the [[Markov chain]] and [[Brownian motion]].

Note that there is a subtle, often overlooked and very important point that is often missed in the plain English statement of the definition: the statespace of the process is constant through time. The conditional description involves a fixed "bandwidth". For example, without this restriction we could augment any process to one which includes the complete history from a given initial condition and it would be made to be Markovian. But the state space would be of increasing dimensionality over time and does not meet the definition.

==History==

{{Main|Markov chain#History}}

==Definition==

There are different formulations of the Markov property in the literature, depending on the assumed level of generality. In the following, some definitions are presented.

=== Markov property in discrete time with discrete state space ===
{{Main|Discrete-time Markov chain}}
A sequence <math>X_1,X_2,\dots</math> of random variables with values in <math>\N</math> possesses the Markov property, if for all <math>x_1,\dots,x_{n+1}\in\N</math>, <math>n\in\N</math>, it holds

<math display="block">P(X_{n+1}=x_{n+1}\mid X_n=x_n,\dots,X_1=x_1) = P(X_{n+1}=x_{n+1}\mid X_n=x_n),</math>

if <math>P(X_n=x_n,\dots,X_1=x_1)>0</math>. In other words, the distribution of <math>X_{n+1}</math> depend solely on the state of <math>X_n</math> and is independent of the state at any time previous to <math>n</math>, which corresponds precisely to the intuition described in the introduction. The Markov property can be defined in the very same way for any finite or [[Countable set|countable]] state space <math>S</math>.

=== Markov property in continuous time with discrete state space ===
Let <math>X=(X_t)_{t\geq 0}</math> be a [[stochastic process]] with values in <math>\N</math>. Then <math>X</math> possesses the Markov property, if for all <math>0\leq t_1<\dots<t_{n+1} </math> and <math>x_1,\dots,x_{n+1}\in\N</math>, <math>n\in\N</math>, and it holds<ref name=":0" />

<math display="block">P(X_{t_{n+1}}=x_{n+1}\mid X_{t_n}=x_n,\dots,X_{t_1}=x_1) = P(X_{t_{n+1}}=x_{n+1}\mid X_{t_n}=x_n),</math>

if <math>P(X_{t_n}=x_n,\dots,X_{t_1}=x_1)>0</math>.

=== Markov property in general ===
The previous definitions can be significantly generalized to a wide class of state spaces and even to different notions of "time" (other than <math>\N</math> and <math>[0,\infty)</math>).

Let <math>(\Omega,\mathcal{F},P)</math> be a [[probability space]] with a [[Filtration (probability theory)|filtration]] <math>(\mathcal{F}_s,\ s \in I)</math>, for some ([[totally ordered]]) index set <math>I</math>; and let <math>(S,\Sigma)</math> be a [[measurable space]]. An <math>(S,\Sigma)</math>-valued stochastic process <math>X=\{X_t:\Omega \to S\}_{t\in I}</math> [[Adapted process|adapted to the filtration]] is said to possess the ''Markov property'' if, for each <math>A \in \Sigma</math>  and each <math>s,t\in I</math> with <math>s<t</math>, it holds<ref>[[Rick Durrett|Durrett, Rick]]. ''Probability: Theory and Examples''. Fourth Edition. [[Cambridge University Press]], 2010.</ref>

:<math>P(X_t \in A \mid \mathcal{F}_s) = P(X_t \in A\mid X_s).</math>


In the case where <math>S</math> is a discrete set with the [[Sigma-algebra#Simple set-based examples|discrete sigma algebra]] and <math>I = \mathbb{N}</math>, this reduces to the discrete Markov property written above.

If <math>I=[0,\infty)</math>, then <math>X</math> is called ''time-homogeneous'' if for all <math>t,s\geq 0</math> the weak Markov property holds:<ref name=":1">{{Cite book |last=Protter |first=Philip |title=Stochastic Integration and Differential Equations |date=1992 |publisher=Springer-Verlag Berlin Heidelberg |isbn=978-3-662-02619-9 |edition=2nd |pages=235–242}}</ref>
:<math>P(X_{t+s}\in A\mid \mathcal F_s)=P(X_t\in A\mid X_0=x)|_{x=X_s}=:P^{X_s}(X_t\in A)</math>.
The newly introduced probability measure <math>P^x(X_t\in \cdot)</math>, <math>x\in S</math>, has the following intuition: It gives the probability that the process <math>X</math> lies in some set at time <math>t</math>, when it was started in <math>x</math> at time zero. The function <math>P_t(x,A):= P^x(X_t\in A)</math>, <math>(t,x,A)\in \R_+\times S\times \Sigma</math>, is also called the ''transition function'' of <math>X</math> and the collection <math>(P_t)_{t\geq 0}</math> its ''transition semigroup''.

==Alternative formulations==

There exists multiple alternative formulations of the elementary Markov property described above. The following are all equivalent:<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Chung |first=Kai Lai |title=Markov Processes, Brownian Motion, and Time Symmetry |last2=Walsh |first2=John B. |publisher=Springer Science+Business Media |year=2005 |isbn=978-0387-22026-0 |edition=2nd |pages=1–5, 47, 49–57,303-304,320-321,325,366}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |author=Øksendal, Bernt K. |author-link=Bernt Øksendal |title=Stochastic Differential Equations: An Introduction with Applications |publisher=Springer, Berlin |year=2003 |isbn=3-540-04758-1}}</ref>

* For all <math>t\geq 0</math> the <math>\sigma</math>-algebras <math>\mathcal F_t</math> and <math>\mathcal F_t' := \sigma(X_s:s\geq t)</math> are [[Conditional independence|conditionally independent]] given <math>X_t</math>. In other words, for all <math>A\in \mathcal F_t</math>, <math>B\in\mathcal F_t'</math>:

<math display="block">P(A\cap B\mid X_t)=P(A\mid X_t)P(B\mid X_t).</math>

* For all <math>t\geq 0</math>, <math>B\in\mathcal F_t'</math>:

<math display="block">P(B\mid \mathcal F_t)=P(B\mid X_t).</math>

* For all <math>t\geq 0</math>, <math>A\in\mathcal F_t</math>:

<math display="block">P(A\mid\mathcal F_t^')=P(A\mid X_t).</math>

* For all <math>t\geq 0</math> and <math>Y:\Omega\rightarrow \mathbb{R}</math> bounded and <math>\mathcal F_t'</math>-measurable

<math display="block">\operatorname{E}[Y\mid\mathcal{F}_t]=\operatorname{E}[Y\mid X_t].</math>

* For all <math>t\geq s\geq 0</math> and <math>f:S\rightarrow \mathbb{R}</math> bounded and measurable

<math display="block">\operatorname{E}[f(X_t)\mid\mathcal{F}_s]=\operatorname{E}[f(X_t)\mid X_s ].</math>

* For all <math>t\geq s\geq 0</math> and <math>f:S\rightarrow \mathbb{R}</math> continuous with compact support

<math display="block">\operatorname{E}[f(X_t)\mid\mathcal{F}_s]=\operatorname{E}[f(X_t)\mid X_s ].</math>

* For all <math>0\leq s_1<...<s_n<s<t</math> and <math>f:S\rightarrow \mathbb{R}</math> continuous with compact support

<math display="block">\operatorname{E}[f(X_t)\mid X_s,X_{s_n},...,X_{s_1}]=\operatorname{E}[f(X_t)\mid X_s].</math>  In particular, if <math>S=\N</math>, then any function <math>f</math> is continuous, and by choosing <math>f=1_{\{x\}} </math> the Markov property for continuous time and discrete state space follows.
If there exists a so-called ''shift-semigroup'' <math>(\theta_t)_{t\geq 0}</math>, i.e., functions <math>\theta_t:\Omega\to\Omega</math> such that

# <math>\theta_0=\mathrm{id}_\Omega</math>,
# <math>\theta_t\circ \theta_s = \theta_{t+s} \quad\forall s,t\geq 0 </math> (semigroup property),
# <math>X_t\circ\theta_s = X_{t+s} \quad\forall s,t\geq 0 </math>,

then the Markov property is equivalent to:<ref name=":0" />

* For all <math>t\geq 0</math> and <math>\Lambda\in\mathcal F_0'</math>

<math display="block">P(\theta_t^{-1}(\Lambda)\mid \mathcal F_t)=P(\theta_t^{-1}(\Lambda)\mid X_t).</math>

* For all <math>t\geq 0</math> and <math>Y:\Omega\rightarrow \mathbb{R}</math> bounded and <math>\mathcal F_0'</math>-measurable

<math display="block">\operatorname{E}[Y\circ\theta_t \mid\mathcal{F}_t]=\operatorname{E}[Y\circ\theta_t\mid X_t].</math>
Depending on the situation, some formulations might be easier to verify or to use than others.

==Strong Markov property==
Suppose that <math>X=(X_t:t\geq 0)</math> is a [[stochastic process]] on a [[probability space]] <math>(\Omega,\mathcal{F},P)</math> with [[natural filtration]] <math>\{\mathcal{F}_t\}_{t\geq 0}</math>. Then for any [[stopping time]] <math> \tau </math> on <math> \Omega </math>, we can define

:<math>\mathcal{F}_{\tau}=\{A \in \mathcal{F}:\forall t \geq 0, \{\tau\leq t\} \cap A \in \mathcal{F}_{t}\}</math>.

Then <math>X</math> is said to have the strong Markov property if, for each [[stopping time]] <math>\tau</math>, conditional on the event <math>\{\tau < \infty\}</math>, we have that for each <math>t\ge 0</math>, <math>X_{\tau + t}</math> is independent of <math>\mathcal{F}_{\tau}</math> given <math>X_\tau</math>. This is equivalent to
:<math>P(X_{\tau+t}\in A, \tau<\infty\mid \mathcal F_\tau)=1_{\{\tau<\infty\}}P(X_t\in A\mid X_0=X_\tau)</math> for all <math>A\in\mathcal F</math>,
where <math>1_{\{\tau<\infty\}}</math> denotes to indicator function of the set <math>\{\tau < \infty\}</math>.

The strong Markov property implies the ordinary Markov property since by taking the stopping time <math>\tau=t</math>, the ordinary Markov property can be deduced.<ref>Ethier, Stewart N. and [[Thomas G. Kurtz|Kurtz, Thomas G.]] ''Markov Processes: Characterization and Convergence''. Wiley Series in Probability and Mathematical Statistics, 1986, p. 158.</ref> The converse is in general not true.

The strong Markov property only leads to non-trivial results in continuous time (i.e., results which do not hold with merely the Markov property), as in the discrete case the strong and the elementary Markov property are equivalent.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Klenke |first=Achim |title=Probability Theory |date=2020 |publisher=Springer Cham |isbn=978-3-030-56402-5 |edition=3rd |pages=397}}</ref>
<!-- Hide for now ... name '''Markov-type property''' seems doubtful
==Markov Type Property==
A stochastic process has a '''Markov-type property''' if the process's [[random variable]]s determine a set of probabilities can be factored in a way that yields the '''Markov property'''. Useful in applied research, members of such classes{{Clarify|October 2009|date=October 2009}} defined by their mathematics or area of application{{Clarify|October 2009|date=October 2009}} are referred to as '''[[Markov random field]]s'''., and occur in many situations. The [[Ising model]] is a prototypical example. -->
== Feller property ==
{{Main|Feller process}}
Although the strong Markov property is in general stronger than the elementary Markov property, it is fulfilled by Markov processes with sufficiently "nice" regularity properties.

A continuous time, homogeneous Markov process is said to have the ''Feller property'', if its transition semigroup <math>(P_t)_{t\geq 0}</math> (see above) fulfills<ref name=":0" />

# <math>P_t f:= \int f(x) P_t(\cdot,dx)\in C_0(S)</math> for all <math>f\in C_0(S)</math>,
# <math>\lim_{t\to 0}\,\lVert P_tf-f\rVert_\infty =0</math> for all <math>f\in C_0(S)</math>,

where <math>C_0(S)</math> denotes the set of [[continuous function]]s [[Vanish at infinity|vanishing at infinity]] and <math>\lVert\cdot\rVert_\infty</math> the [[Uniform norm|sup norm]].

== Implications ==

=== Discrete time ===
{{Main|Markov chain#Properties}}

=== Continuous time ===
In continuous time, the elementary Markov property is a rather weak condition and does not imply particularly interesting properties other than maybe the fact that for a Markov process <math>X=(X_t)_{t\geq 0}</math> the reverse process <math>(X_{T-t})_{t\geq 0}</math> from a time <math>T>0</math> has again the Markov property.<ref name=":0" />

If <math>X</math> is time-homogeneous and fulfills the weak Markov property, then already a few more statements can be made.

* The law of the process on the path space <math>(\R^{[0,\infty)},\mathcal B(\R)^{\otimes[0,\infty)})</math> is uniquely determined by its transition semigroup <math>(P_t)_{t\geq 0}</math> and the distribution of <math>X_0</math>.
* For any <math>\alpha>0</math> and bounded, non-negative, measurable function <math>f</math>, the process

<math display="block">Z_t = e^{-\alpha t}\operatorname E^{X_t}\Big[\int_0^\infty e^{-\alpha s}f(X_s)\mathrm ds\Big], \qquad t\geq 0,</math>is a [[Martingale (probability theory)#Submartingales, supermartingales, and relationship to harmonic functions|supermartingale]]<ref>{{Cite book |last=Le Gall |first=Jean-François |title=Brownian Motion, Martingales, and Stochastic Calculus |publisher=[[Springer Science+Business Media|Springer]] |year=2016 |isbn=978-3-319-31088-6 |pages=157}}</ref> and
<math display="block">Y_t = \int_0^t e^{-\alpha s}f(X_s)\mathrm ds + e^{-\alpha t}\operatorname E^{X_t}\Big[\int_0^\infty e^{-\alpha s}f(X_s)\mathrm ds\Big], \qquad t\geq 0,</math> is a [[Uniform integrability|uniformly integrable]] [[Martingale (probability theory)|martingale]].<ref name=":0" />

However, the weak Markov property alone is still too general to imply much more than the above properties. Most statements on Markov processes require the [[Feller process|Feller property]] (see above), which provides more regularity of the transition semigroup.

In the following, let <math>X</math> be a Feller process, that is, a time-homogeneous Markov process with the Feller property, in a filtration <math>(\mathcal F_t)_{t\geq 0}</math> with values in a [[Polish space]] <math>S</math> and <math>(P_t)_{t\geq 0}</math> being its transition semigroup.

==== Path properties ====
If the filtration <math>(\mathcal F_t)_{t\geq 0}</math> is [[Filtration (probability theory)#Augmented filtration|augmented]], then <math>X</math> has a [[Stochastic process#Modification|modification]] with right-continuous (even [[càdlàg]]) paths, and this modification has the strong Markov property.<ref name=":0" /> Thus, Feller processes are often assumed to be right-continuous strong Markov processes without further mention. 

==== Dynkin formula ====
{{Main|Dynkin's formula}}
Let <math>\tau</math> be any [[stopping time]] such that <math>\operatorname E[\tau]<\infty</math> and let <math>f\in C_0(S)</math> be such that

<math display="block">Af(x) := \lim_{t\to 0}\frac{\operatorname E^x[f(X_t)]-f(x)}{t} , \qquad x\in S,</math>

exists (<math>A</math> is the [[Infinitesimal generator (stochastic processes)|infinitesimal generator]] of <math>X</math>). Then, for all <math>x\in S</math>,

<math display="block">\operatorname E^x[f(X_\tau)] = f(x) + \operatorname E^x\Big[\int_0^\tau Af(X_t)\mathrm dt\Big].</math>

==== Recurrence and transience ====
For a set <math>A\subset S</math>, one might be interested in the question whether the process will return infinitely often to the set <math>A</math>. Defining the set of paths under which the later holds as

<math display="block">R(A):=\left\{\limsup_{t\to\infty}1_A(X_t)=1\right\},</math>

the set <math>A</math> is called ''recurrent'', if <math>P(R(A))=1</math>, and ''transient'', if <math>P(R(A))=0</math>.

In general, a set may be neither recurrent nor transient. For Feller processes, however, the following two conditions are equivalent.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Revuz |first=Daniel |title=Continuous Martingales and Brownian Motion |last2=Yor |first2=Marc |publisher=Springer |year=2005 |isbn=978-3-642-08400-3 |edition=3rd |pages=423-424}}</ref>

* Every bounded function <math>f</math> (on <math>\Omega</math>) that is invariant with respect to the shift, that is, <math>f\circ\theta_t=f</math> for all <math>t\geq 0</math>, is already constant.
* Every set is either recurrent or transient.

==== Doob's ''h''-transform ====
{{Main|Doob's h-transform}}
The strong Markov property is conserved under an <math>h</math>-transform–a method introduced by [[Joseph L. Doob|J.L. Doob]] to manipulate Markov processes. For a function <math>h:S\to (0,\infty)</math> fulfilling

<math display="block">\operatorname E[h(X_t)] = \int_S h(y)P_t(x,\mathrm dy) = h(x), \qquad \forall x\in S,\, t\geq 0,</math>

the <math>h</math>-transformed process <math>X^h</math> is the (homogeneous) Markov process with transition function

<math display="block">P^h_t(x,A) =
\frac{1}{h(x)}\int_A h(y)P_t(x,\mathrm dy),\qquad\forall x\in S,\, A\in \mathcal B(S),\,t\geq 0.</math>

As mentioned above, if <math>\tilde X</math> is a right-continuous modification of the original process <math>X</math> with the strong Markov property, then its <math>h</math>-transform <math>\tilde X^h</math> is a right-continuous strong Markov process as well.<ref name=":0" />

==== Time reversal ====
Let <math>\tilde X</math> be a right-continuous modification of the original process <math>X</math> with the strong Markov property and suppose <math>\tilde X</math> is killed at a random time <math>\xi</math> with <math>P(\xi<\infty)>0</math> (this means that for <math>t\geq\xi</math> the process is sent to a so-called cemetery point <math>\partial\notin S</math>) in such a way that the killed process is still a homogeneous Markov process. Then the reverse process

<math display="block">\overset{\leftarrow}{X_t}(\omega) = \begin{cases}
\tilde X_{\xi-t}(\omega), && \text{ if } 0< t\leq \xi(\omega), \\
\partial, && \text{ if } t>\xi(\omega)\text{ or }\xi(\omega)=\infty
\end{cases}</math>

is a left-continuous homogeneous Markov process with semigroup <math>(\overset{\leftarrow}{P_t})_{t\geq 0}</math>. If <math>\overset{\leftarrow}{P_t}</math> and <math>P_t</math> are understood as operators <math>P_t:f\mapsto \int_S f(x)P_t(\cdot,\mathrm dx)</math>, then <math>\overset{\leftarrow}{P_t}</math> is the [[Hermitian adjoint|adjoint]] of <math>P_t</math> with respect to the [[scalar product]] induced by the measure

<math display="block">G(A) = \int_0^\infty \operatorname E[P_t(\tilde X_0,A)]\mathrm dt, \qquad A\in\mathcal B(S),</math>

in the sense

<math display="block">\langle \overset{\leftarrow}{P_t}f,g\rangle_G = \langle f,P_tg\rangle_G = \int_S f(x)P_tg(x) \mathrm dG(x)</math>

for all continuous functions <math>f,g\in C(S)</math>.<ref name=":0" /> 

Moreover, if there exists a measure <math>\nu</math> such that <math>\langle P_t f,g\rangle_\nu = \langle f,P_t g\rangle_\nu</math> (in this case <math>\tilde X</math> is called ''self-dual'') and the measure <math>G</math> is [[Absolutely continuous probability distribution|absolutely continuous]] with respect to <math>\nu</math>, then <math>\overset{\leftarrow}{X}</math> has the same transition probabilities as the <math>h</math>-transform <math>\tilde X^h</math> with <math>h= \mathrm dG/\mathrm d\nu</math>. So in particular, if <math>\tilde X^h_0</math> and <math>\overset{\leftarrow}{X_0}</math> have the same distribution, then <math>\overset{\leftarrow}{X}</math>and <math>\tilde X^h</math> are the same process.<ref name=":0" />

==Examples==

=== Intuitive example ===
Assume that an urn contains two red balls and one green ball. One ball was drawn yesterday, one ball was drawn today, and the final ball will be drawn tomorrow. All of the draws are "without replacement".

Suppose you know that today's ball was red, but you have no information about yesterday's ball. The chance that tomorrow's ball will be red is 1/2. That's because the only two remaining outcomes for this random experiment are:

{| class="wikitable"
|-
! align="center" | Day !! align="center" | Outcome 1 !! align="center" | Outcome 2
|-
| align="center" | Yesterday || align="center" | Red || align="center" | Green
|-
| align="center" | Today || align="center" | Red || align="center" | Red
|-
| align="center"| Tomorrow || align="center" | Green || align="center" | Red
|}

On the other hand, if you know that both today and yesterday's balls were red, then you are guaranteed to get a green ball tomorrow.

This discrepancy shows that the probability distribution for tomorrow's color depends not only on the present value, but is also affected by information about the past. This stochastic process of observed colors doesn't have the Markov property. Using the same experiment above, if sampling "without replacement" is changed to sampling "with replacement," the process of observed colors will have the Markov property.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://math.stackexchange.com/q/89394 |title=Example of a stochastic process which does not have the Markov property |publisher=[[Stack Exchange]] | access-date= 2020-07-07}}</ref>

=== Stochastic processes ===
Many prominent stochastic processes are Markov processes: The [[Brownian motion]], the [[Brownian bridge]], the [[Doléans-Dade exponential|stochastic exponential]], the [[Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process|Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process]] and the [[Poisson point process|Poisson process]] have the Markov property.

More generally, any semimartingale <math>X</math> with values in <math>\R^n</math> that is given by the [[stochastic differential equation]]

:<math>X_t = X_0 + \sum_{i=1}^d \Big[\int_0^t g_i(X_s)ds + \int_0^t f_i(X_s)dB_s^i \Big]</math>,

where <math>B=(B^1,...,B^d)</math> is a <math>d</math>-dimensional Brownian motion and <math>f_1,...,f_d,g_1,...,g_d:\R^n\to\R^n</math> are autonomous (i.e., they do not depend on time) Lipschitz functions, is time-homogeneous and has the strong Markov property. If<math>f_1,...,f_d,g_1,...,g_d</math> are not autonomous, then <math>X</math> still has the elementary Markov property.<ref name=":1" />

== Applications ==

=== Forecasting ===
In the fields of [[predictive modelling]] and [[probabilistic forecasting]], the Markov property is considered desirable since it may enable the reasoning and resolution of the problem that otherwise would not be possible to be resolved because of its [[Intractability (complexity)|intractability]]. Such a model is known as a [[Markov model]].

=== Markov Chain Monte Carlo ===
An application of the Markov property in a generalized form is in [[Markov chain Monte Carlo]] computations in the context of [[Bayesian statistics]].
